blocks.text: Say you are tracking your coffee shop's daily sales. Some days are slow, some days spike because of a local event, and just eyeballing the raw numbers day by day tells you almost nothing about the actual trend. What you really want is something smoother, a sense of how the last few days have been doing together, not just today in isolation and not the average of the entire month either. That in between view, computed one row at a time but using a handful of nearby rows, is exactly what a window function gives you.
This lesson walks through the two core tools pandas gives you for this, .rolling() and .expanding(), what a window function actually means at its core, and where each one shows up in real data work.

blocks.alt: A column of values feeding into a nearby window of rows which produces one output value per row
blocks.caption: The whole idea in one picture: a window function looks at a row and its neighbors, and produces one answer per row.

blocks.text: 1. Introduction

At its core, a window function is an operation computed over a sliding or expanding subset of nearby rows, rather than the whole column at once or one row in total isolation. It sits in between two operations you already know well from earlier in this course.

items: An elementwise operation looks at exactly one row and produces one output for that row, completely ignorant of every other row around it, like multiplying a whole column by two.
An aggregation looks at the entire column at once and collapses it down to a single value, like the average of every day's sales across a whole year.
A window function looks at a row plus a handful of its neighbors and produces one output per row, informed by, but not identical to, either extreme above.

blocks.text: Put differently, a window function keeps the one output per row shape of an elementwise operation, but each output is computed using more than just that one row's value. That is the whole trick, and pandas gives you two main ways to define what "nearby" means.

blocks.alt: Three flowchart branches showing an elementwise operation, an aggregation, and a window function and what each one produces
blocks.caption: An elementwise operation looks at one row, an aggregation looks at the whole column, a window function looks at a row plus its neighbors.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: Moving averages, running totals, rolling volatility, and trailing counts are all window functions under the hood. Anywhere you have heard the phrase moving average or running total, a window function is doing the actual work.

blocks.text: A quick side by side in actual pandas code makes the distinction stick even better than any diagram can.

code.content:
prices = pd.Series([10, 12, 11, 15, 14])

prices * 2                          # elementwise: one output per row, no neighbors involved
prices.mean()                       # aggregation: the whole column collapses to one number
prices.rolling(window=2).mean()     # window function: one output per row, using a neighbor

blocks.text: 2. Rolling Windows: A Fixed Size Sliding Window

The most common window function in pandas is .rolling(). It builds a fixed size window, meaning the window always covers exactly the same number of rows, and slides that window forward one row at a time as it moves down the column.
You have almost certainly already seen the result of a rolling window even if you never called it that. A few very familiar examples:

items: A stock's 50 day moving average, smoothing out day to day noise in the price chart.
A fitness tracker showing your trailing 7 day average step count instead of one noisy daily number.
A sensor reading system that smooths out jittery raw measurements by averaging the last few readings together.

blocks.text: 2.1 How .rolling Works

Calling .rolling(window=3) on a pandas Series or DataFrame column sets up a window that always covers 3 rows: the current row and the 2 rows directly before it. Chaining an aggregation like .mean() onto that tells pandas exactly what to compute inside each window as it slides forward.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

sales = pd.Series([120, 135, 128, 150, 142, 160], name="daily_sales")
rolling_avg = sales.rolling(window=3).mean()
print(rolling_avg)

blocks.text: Run this and you will see the first two rows come back as NaN. There simply are not 3 rows available yet to fill the window. More on exactly why that happens, and how to change it, in a moment.

blocks.alt: Three overlapping windows each covering 3 rows sliding forward one row at a time down a column
blocks.caption: The window always covers 3 rows, but which 3 rows keeps shifting forward as you move down the column.

blocks.text: 2.2 A Worked Example
Let's make the sliding mechanic completely tangible with the coffee shop numbers from above. Here are 6 days of sales, in dollars, and the 3 day rolling average pandas computes for each one.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Day","Daily sales","Rolling 3 day average"],"rows":[["Day 1","120","NaN, not enough rows yet"],["Day 2","135","NaN, still not enough rows yet"],["Day 3","128","127.67, the average of 120, 135, and 128"],["Day 4","150","137.67, the average of 135, 128, and 150"],["Day 5","142","140.0, the average of 128, 150, and 142"],["Day 6","160","150.67, the average of 150, 142, and 160"]]}

blocks.alt: Day 1 and day 2 producing no result yet while day 3 produces the first rolling average of 127.67
blocks.caption: The window needs all 3 rows filled before it can produce its first real result, which lands on day 3.

blocks.text: Notice the pattern: day 4's average drops day 1 out of the window entirely and picks up day 4 instead. The window is not accumulating everything it has ever seen, it is a strict 3 row snapshot that continually swaps its oldest row for the newest one as it slides forward.
2.3 The min_periods Parameter

By default, .rolling() insists the window be completely full before it will produce a result at all, which is exactly why day 1 and day 2 came back as NaN above. There simply were not 3 values available yet. The min_periods parameter lets you relax that rule.

With min_periods=1, pandas will happily compute an average from whatever rows are actually available inside the window, even if that is only 1 or 2 rows instead of the full 3. Day 1 now returns 120.0 by itself, and day 2 returns the average of 120 and 135, which is 127.5.

blocks.title: NaN at the start is normal, not a bug
blocks.content: Seeing NaN in the first few rows of a rolling calculation is expected behavior, not something broken in your data. It just means the default min_periods equals the full window size. Decide deliberately whether you want that strictness or whether min_periods=1 fits your use case better.

blocks.alt: Default min_periods producing NaN for the first two rows compared with min_periods of 1 producing a partial average instead
blocks.caption: Same data, same window size, two different answers for how to handle the start of the series.

blocks.text: 3. Expanding Windows: A Window That Only Grows

Where .rolling() keeps a fixed size window, .expanding() does the opposite. It starts with just the first row and keeps growing to include every row from the start of the series up through the current row, never shrinking, never dropping old rows out.
3.1 How .expanding Works
The syntax mirrors .rolling() closely, you just drop the window size entirely, since an expanding window does not have a fixed size to begin with.

At row 1 the window is just row 1. At row 2 it is rows 1 and 2 together. By row 6 it is all 6 rows at once. An expanding sum is nothing more than a running total, and an expanding mean is a running average that includes everything seen so far.

blocks.alt: An expanding window growing from row 1 to include rows 1 and 2, then rows 1 through 3, then rows 1 through 4
blocks.caption: The expanding window never drops a row. It only ever adds the next one on top.

blocks.text: 3.2 The Running Bank Balance Analogy

The clearest way to feel this in your gut is your own bank balance. Every transaction changes your balance, but your balance is never just today's transaction in isolation, it is the running total of every deposit and withdrawal you have ever made up to this point. That running total is precisely what an expanding sum computes.

code.content:
transactions = pd.Series([100, 50, -30, 20, -10], name="transaction")
balance = transactions.expanding().sum()
print(balance)

blocks.alt: Three transactions each folding into a running bank balance total that never resets
blocks.caption: Each new transaction adds onto everything that came before it, exactly like an expanding sum.

blocks.text: 3.3 Rolling Versus Expanding at a Glance

Stated plainly, side by side: rolling has a fixed size window that slides forward, always covering the same number of rows and dropping old ones as new ones arrive. Expanding has a window that only grows, it never shrinks and it never drops a row once that row has entered the window.

blocks.caption: Same underlying idea, two very different shapes: a box that slides versus a box that only ever grows.

blocks.text: 4. Beyond the Mean: Other Aggregations

Nothing about .rolling() or .expanding() limits you to .mean(). Both are just window builders. You can chain almost any aggregation function you like onto either one, exactly like you would on a plain aggregation.
4.1 sum, std, max, and More
Swap out the aggregation at the end of the chain and you get a completely different rolling statistic, still computed over the same sliding 3 row window.

code.content:
sales.rolling(window=3).sum()    # total sales over the last 3 days
sales.rolling(window=3).std()    # how spread out the last 3 days were
sales.rolling(window=3).max()    # the best single day within the last 3

blocks.text: A rolling sum tells you the total over the window instead of the average. A rolling standard deviation tells you how volatile or steady the last few values have been, useful for spotting a sudden noisy stretch. A rolling max tells you the best value seen within the window, handy for tracking recent peaks or streaks. Running all three on the same coffee shop sales gives you three different lenses on the same 3 day window.

blocks.alt: One rolling window of 3 rows feeding into three different aggregations, sum, standard deviation, and max
blocks.caption: Same window, three different questions answered: total, spread, and peak.

blocks.title: The same idea applies to expanding
blocks.content: expanding().sum(), expanding().std(), and expanding().max() all work exactly the same way, just against a window that keeps growing instead of staying a fixed size.

blocks.text: 5. Rolling Windows on Grouped Data

Real datasets are rarely just one uninterrupted series. More often you have multiple categories mixed together in one DataFrame, stores, users, products, and you want a rolling calculation computed separately within each one rather than smeared across all of them combined.
5.1 groupby Then rolling
Chain .rolling() straight onto a groupby() result and pandas computes the window independently inside every group.

This computes a completely independent 3 row rolling average inside store A and inside store B. Store B's first two rows never get mixed into store A's rolling window, even though the two stores sit right next to each other in the original DataFrame. Without the groupby, a rolling window would slide straight across the boundary between the two stores and produce a meaningless blended average.

blocks.alt: Store A rows producing a rolling average inside store A only, and store B rows producing a separate rolling average inside store B only
blocks.caption: The rolling window resets at every group boundary, it never leaks across from one store into the next.

blocks.title: Watch the index
blocks.content: groupby followed by rolling hands you back a result indexed by both the group and the original row position. If you want it lined up flat against your original DataFrame, you typically drop the group level with something like reset_index(level=0, drop=True) before assigning it back as a plain column.

blocks.text: 6. Worked Example: Rolling and Expanding Side by Side
Let's put both windows on the same small dataset so the contrast is completely obvious. Back to the coffee shop's 6 days of sales.

code.content:
sales = pd.Series([120, 135, 128, 150, 142, 160], name="daily_sales")

comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "daily_sales": sales,
    "rolling_3day_avg": sales.rolling(window=3).mean(),
    "expanding_running_total": sales.expanding().sum(),
})
print(comparison)

blocks.alt: The same six daily sales values feeding into a rolling 3 day average column and a separate expanding running total column
blocks.caption: Same input, two very different outputs: a local 3 day smoothing versus a total that only ever climbs.

blocks.text: Look at how differently the two columns behave. The rolling average column keeps forgetting the oldest day as a new one arrives, it is a local, reactive smoothing of just the last 3 days. The expanding column never forgets anything, it just keeps piling every day on top of the last, which is why it climbs steadily larger by day 6.
7. Wrapping Up

A window function fills the gap between an elementwise operation that only ever sees one row and an aggregation that collapses an entire column into a single number. .rolling() gives you a fixed size window that slides forward, .expanding() gives you a window that only grows, and both accept whatever aggregation actually fits your problem, not just mean.

items: A window function computes over a sliding or expanding subset of nearby rows, producing one output per row.
rolling(window=n) keeps a fixed size window and slides it forward one row at a time.
min_periods controls whether a window needs to be completely full before it produces a result.
expanding() grows from the first row up through the current row and never shrinks.
Both rolling and expanding accept sum, std, max, and plenty of other aggregations beyond mean.
groupby("category").rolling(3) computes the window independently inside each group.

blocks.title: Where this goes next
blocks.content: Everything here treated the window purely in terms of row position, the current row and however many rows sit before it. Later in this course, the Time Series with Pandas module comes back to rolling and expanding windows in far more depth, this time anchored to real datetime data, with time based window sizes like 7 days or 30 minutes instead of a fixed row count. Everything you just learned here is the foundation that module builds on.
